moose.anatomy: A moose looks almost mismatched: long legs, a short neck, a humped back, and a long face with an overhanging, flexible upper lip that strips leaves from branches. That big nose is more than it seems; it contains a large, complex nasal cavity, and moose can close their nostrils when they put their heads underwater to feed. Under the chin hangs a flap of skin called a bell or dewlap, whose purpose is still debated. Their coat is made of long, hollow guard hairs over a woolly undercoat, excellent insulation in winter but a problem in summer heat, which is one reason moose spend so much time in water. Long legs let them step over fallen logs and walk through snow up to about 90 centimetres deep. A bull's broad, palm-shaped antlers can weigh over 30 kilograms and are grown in about five months each year.
moose.family: Moose mate in September and October, the season called the rut. Bulls stop eating much, call with deep grunts, thrash bushes with their antlers and sometimes fight rivals by locking antlers and shoving. Cows call with long, moaning wails. After about eight months, in late May or June, the cow gives birth to one calf, sometimes twins, in a sheltered spot, often near water. Calves are reddish-brown and can stand within a day. They grow fast on rich milk, gaining well over a kilogram a day, and can outrun a person within a few days. The mother is fiercely protective, and the calf stays with her for about a year, until she drives it away shortly before her next calf is born. Wolves and bears take many calves, so their first year is the most dangerous.
moose.people: The name 'moose' comes from an Algonquian word, often translated as 'twig eater' or 'he strips off'. For thousands of years moose have been a major source of meat, hide, sinew and bone for Indigenous peoples across the North, and hunting remains important in many communities today. Moose are hugely popular with wildlife watchers, and parks such as Algonquin in Ontario draw visitors hoping to see one by the road. They can also be dangerous: collisions between cars and moose are a serious hazard in Newfoundland, Scandinavia and elsewhere, and a frightened or protective moose can charge. Moose were introduced to Newfoundland in 1904, where only a handful were released, and there are now over 100,000. Wildlife biologists track moose health closely, studying the effects of ticks, parasites and warming winters.

snapping-turtle.anatomy: The common snapping turtle has a large head, a powerful hooked beak and long neck that can shoot forward surprisingly far, reaching nearly halfway back along its own shell. The top shell, or carapace, has three ridges of bumps that wear smoother with age and is often coated with algae, which helps with camouflage. The bottom shell, the plastron, is small and cross-shaped, leaving the legs free but offering little protection, which is why snappers rely on their bite. Their long tail has a row of saw-like plates along the top. Snappers have strong claws for digging and walking along the bottom; they are poor swimmers compared with many turtles and usually walk underwater instead. They have good night vision and an excellent sense of smell, and can sense vibrations through the water. Their bite is strong, but they rarely bite anything they don't intend to eat.
snapping-turtle.family: Snapping turtles mate in spring and summer, often in the water. In late May and June, females leave the water to find sunny, sandy or gravelly spots to dig nests, often road shoulders, railway beds or gardens, sometimes travelling more than a kilometre. A female digs a flask-shaped hole with her back legs and lays between about 20 and 40 round, white eggs, sometimes more, then covers them and leaves. Raccoons, skunks and foxes dig up many nests. Those that survive hatch in late summer or early autumn; in the coldest places the hatchlings may stay in the nest over winter. Nest temperature decides their sex: cooler and warmer extremes produce females, while middle temperatures produce males. The hatchlings, about the size of a coin, head straight for water. Very few survive to adulthood.
snapping-turtle.people: Snapping turtles have a fearsome reputation, but most people never encounter one unless they meet a female crossing a road in June. In many places, especially Ontario, people help them cross safely: lifting them carefully by the back of the shell with both hands, or nudging them along with a car mat, always in the direction they were going. Picking one up by the tail can hurt its spine. Some Indigenous creation stories describe the world being formed on the back of a great turtle, and North America is called Turtle Island by many Indigenous peoples. Snapping turtles have been hunted for food in parts of their range, and in Ontario hunting them was finally banned in 2017 because adults are so slow to replace. Turtle rescue centres now treat injured turtles and even incubate eggs from females killed on roads.

spring-peeper.anatomy: A spring peeper is a tiny tree frog, tan, brown or grey with a darker X-shaped mark across its back and a dark band between the eyes. Its skin can lighten or darken slightly to match its surroundings. Its fingers and toes end in round, sticky pads that let it climb grass stems and shrubs, although it spends most of its time near the ground. A male has a dark throat and a vocal sac that inflates like a balloon, almost as big as the frog itself, when it calls; the sac amplifies the sound so a single peeper can be heard far away. Like other frogs, the peeper breathes through its lungs and through its moist skin, and drinks by absorbing water through the skin of its belly. Its large eyes face forward and sideways, helping it judge distance when it leaps on insects.
spring-peeper.family: In early spring, as soon as ice melts from ponds and flooded woods, males gather and call through the night. Each 'peep' takes a lot of energy, and males may call thousands of times an evening. Females choose males, often preferring faster or louder calls. Mating happens in shallow water, where the female lays around 800 to 1,000 eggs, one at a time or in small clusters, attached to underwater plants. The eggs hatch in about a week. The tadpoles feed on algae and tiny bits of plant matter and change into tiny frogs in two to three months, leaving the water in early summer. Many breeding pools are temporary and dry up by midsummer, which keeps out fish that would eat eggs and tadpoles, but also means tadpoles race against the water drying up.
spring-peeper.people: For many people in eastern Canada and the United States, the first peepers of the year are a beloved sign that winter is truly over, and in New England they are sometimes called 'pinkletinks'. Because they rely on small seasonal wetlands, peepers are used in volunteer frog-call surveys run in many provinces and states. Volunteers drive set routes on spring nights, stopping to listen and record which frog species are calling and how loudly, giving scientists a picture of how wetlands are faring year to year. Scientists studying how animals survive freezing have also learned a lot from frogs like peepers and wood frogs. Their natural antifreeze is of interest to medical researchers looking for better ways to preserve human organs and tissues for transplant.

american-lobster.anatomy: An American lobster has a hard outer skeleton made of chitin, a tough natural material also found in insect shells, and calcium, ten legs, and a long, muscular tail that ends in a fan. The first pair of legs carries the claws: a heavy, blunt crusher claw for breaking shells and a thinner cutter claw with sharp teeth for tearing. Lobsters can be right- or left-'handed', depending on which side the crusher grows. Their eyes sit on movable stalks and are good at detecting motion in dim light, though not detail. Long antennae feel their surroundings, while the short, branched antennules sample the water for scents, and tiny hairs on their walking legs and mouthparts taste food. Lobsters breathe through feathery gills tucked under the shell along their sides. Their blood is colourless or slightly blue because, like an octopus, they use copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen.
american-lobster.family: A female lobster mates soon after she molts, while her shell is still soft. She stores sperm and later fertilises her eggs as she lays them, gluing thousands to the underside of her tail, where they are called 'berries'. A large female can carry tens of thousands of eggs. She carries and cleans them for about 9 to 11 months, fanning them with water. When they hatch, the tiny larvae float near the surface for several weeks, drifting with the currents, molting several times; most are eaten by fish. Survivors settle to the bottom, where they hide in rocky crevices. Lobsters grow slowly and may take five to eight years to reach the size allowed for harvest. Older lobsters molt less often, perhaps once every year or two, and big ones may be decades old.
american-lobster.people: In colonial New England and the Maritimes, lobsters were so abundant they washed up on beaches in piles and were fed to servants and prisoners and used as fertiliser. That changed in the 1800s with canning and railways, which let lobster be shipped inland, and today it is a luxury food and one of the most valuable fisheries in Canada and the United States, central to the economy and identity of many coastal towns. Fishers use rules to keep stocks healthy: minimum and maximum sizes, limited licences and seasons, and the practice of notching the tail of egg-bearing females and returning them so they can keep breeding. Scientists and fishers together track how warming water is shifting lobster populations, pushing them northward toward Atlantic Canada and away from southern New England.

snow-leopard.anatomy: The snow leopard is a medium-sized big cat with a thick, smoky-grey to cream coat covered in dark rosettes and spots. Its fur can be up to 12 centimetres long on the belly, and its tail, almost as long as its body, is thick and furry. Its paws are large and wide, with fur on the soles that keeps them warm and spreads its weight on snow. Its forelimbs are short and powerful and its hind limbs long, giving it strength and agility for leaping across rocky slopes. The large nasal cavity warms cold air before it reaches the lungs. Its eyes are pale green or grey, unusual among big cats. Snow leopards' voice boxes are built differently from those of lions and tigers, so they can't roar, so they communicate with hisses, growls, mews and a puffing sound called chuffing.
snow-leopard.family: Snow leopards mate in late winter, and the female gives birth after about three months, usually to two or three cubs, in a rocky den lined with her own fur. Cubs are born blind and helpless and open their eyes after about a week. They start eating meat at around two months and leave the den with their mother at about three months. For the next year and a half, she teaches them to hunt, and the family travels together across her territory. At around 18 to 22 months, the young become independent and leave to find their own range, which can be a dangerous time as they wander into areas with livestock and people. Males take no part in raising cubs. A female may have only a few litters in her lifetime.
snow-leopard.people: Snow leopards have long been part of the cultures of Central and South Asia. In parts of the Himalayas, people see them as sacred, and Buddhist monasteries in the region help protect them. It appears on the emblems of cities such as Almaty and Bishkek, and both Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan treat it as a national symbol. Because they live in such remote mountains, they were rarely photographed until camera traps became common, and researchers now use these cameras, DNA from droppings and satellite collars to study them. Herders sometimes kill snow leopards after losing livestock. Conservation groups have reduced this by helping communities build predator-proof livestock pens, set up insurance schemes that compensate losses, and earn income from crafts and wildlife tourism, giving people a reason to keep snow leopards alive.

red-panda.anatomy: A red panda is about the size of a large house cat, with thick rusty-red fur on its back, black legs and belly, and a long, bushy tail ringed with red and buff stripes. Its face is white with reddish 'tear' marks running from each eye, and it has upright, white-edged ears. The dark belly and legs may help camouflage it when seen from below against the dark canopy. Its fur is dense, and even the soles of its feet are furry, protecting them from cold and wet branches. Its sharp, semi-retractable claws and flexible ankles make it a superb climber. Red pandas have strong jaws and broad molar teeth for crushing bamboo, but their digestive system is short and simple, like a carnivore's, so they extract only a small fraction of the energy in what they eat.
red-panda.family: Red pandas are solitary for most of the year and meet only to mate, in winter. After a pregnancy that can last from about three to five months, because the development of the embryo can be delayed, the female gives birth in early summer to one to four cubs, usually two, in a nest in a tree hollow or rock crevice. Before birth, she gathers leaves, moss and twigs to line it. The cubs are born with thick grey-buff fur and closed eyes, and open them at around three weeks. They stay in the nest for about three months, while the mother returns regularly to feed and clean them. They are weaned at around six to eight months and stay with her until the next breeding season, when they leave to find territories of their own.
red-panda.people: The red panda was described by Western science in 1825, decades before the giant panda, and the word 'panda' probably comes from a Nepali name for it. In parts of Nepal and India, red pandas appear in local beliefs and are considered good luck. They are popular in zoos around the world, and international breeding programs keep a healthy captive population. The red panda is the state animal of Sikkim in India, and the Firefox web browser's name refers to it, since 'firefox' is one of its nicknames. In Nepal, the Red Panda Network trains local 'forest guardians', who monitor red pandas, help restore forest, and teach communities about them. Ecotourism treks to see wild red pandas give villagers income from protecting forests rather than clearing them.

sunda-pangolin.anatomy: The Sunda pangolin is covered from head to tail in overlapping brownish scales, except for its face, belly and inner legs, which are covered in skin and sparse hair. The scales are made of keratin and grow throughout its life, worn down as it digs and climbs. It has a small, cone-shaped head, tiny eyes and poor eyesight, but an excellent sense of smell for finding ant and termite nests. Its front feet have long, curved claws for ripping into nests, so it walks on its knuckles or on its hind legs to protect them. Its long, sticky tongue starts deep in its chest and is coated with thick saliva. Without teeth, it relies on a muscular stomach with tough spines and swallowed stones to grind its food. Its prehensile tail can grip branches, helping it climb trees with ease.
sunda-pangolin.family: Sunda pangolins live alone and meet only to mate. After a pregnancy of around six months, the female usually gives birth to a single baby, sometimes two, often in a burrow or tree hollow. The newborn's scales are soft at first and harden within a couple of days. For the first weeks, the baby stays in the den while the mother forages. Later it rides on her back or tail as she travels and climbs, gripping tightly. If danger threatens, the mother curls into a ball around her young one, sheltering it inside her armour. The young pangolin learns to find food by following its mother and is weaned at about three or four months, staying with her until it is ready to live on its own. Pangolins breed slowly, so populations recover poorly from hunting.
sunda-pangolin.people: Pangolins have been eaten as bushmeat and used in traditional medicine across Asia for a very long time, with their scales wrongly believed to cure ailments from poor circulation to skin disease. In recent decades, demand has turned this into a vast illegal trade, with tonnes of scales seized at ports, and the Sunda pangolin is now critically endangered. Since 2017, all eight pangolin species have been listed on Appendix I of CITES, the international treaty that controls the wildlife trade, which bans international commercial trade, and China removed pangolin scales from its official list of traditional medicines in 2020. Rescue centres in Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia care for pangolins confiscated from traffickers, and some are released back into protected forests. World Pangolin Day, held each February, raises awareness of these little-known animals.
